I can't give you a revenue figure for the last three months, because MI Health Ltd's accounting data isn't loaded into this system. To be precise about what happened: for 1 July to 30 September 2026 the P&L returned `DATA_NOT_AVAILABLE` with a null value for revenue, gross profit, operating expenses, and net profit — not zero. I also checked the full six-month window to 30 September, the balance sheet as at that date, the cash balances, and a sweep of all invoices, bills, and bank transactions. Every one of them came back empty or null: zero bank accounts, zero cash transactions, zero invoice and bill records, and a balance sheet summary of nil across total assets, total liabilities, and net assets.

This corrects something I reported earlier in this session. I previously gave you a revenue total of GBP 0 with0% margins. That was wrong, and I should not have stated it. The difference matters: a genuine GBP 0 tells you the company recorded sales and none of them landed, which points at a data or posting problem somewhere specific. A null here means there is nothing posted at all, which is an entirely different diagnosis.

Worth noting that the tenant itself is configured and active, not broken. MI Health Ltd is registered in GB, reports in GBP, is tax-registered, and carries a 31 March financial year end, so the July-to-September window you asked about does sit correctly inside the current fiscal year. The gap is purely in the transactional data.

The most likely explanations are that no accounting package has been connected to this tenant yet, or that a connection exists but has never been synced. Until one of those is resolved I won't be able to give you reliable figures on revenue, profitability, cash position, or receivables — and I'd treat any number I produced from this tenant right now as unreliable rather than zero.

Once the data is connected, ask me again for the July to September window and I'll pull the P&L and break the revenue down by customer and product. In the meantime, if you can tell me which system the ledger lives in, I can help you work out the connection.

I can't give you a cash figure, and I want to be direct about why rather than report a number that would mislead you.

The cash balance call returned £0 with an empty list of bank accounts. That zero is not a real figure — it's the absence of data. The balance sheet for the same date returns every metric tagged `DATA_NOT_AVAILABLE`, with cash flow figures marked `NOT_AVAILABLE` and the reason given as "Bank transactions report unavailable for period." A cash transaction search across all directions returns zero records, the chart of accounts is empty, and the six-month cash flow summary comes back with no monthly trends at all. If MI Health Ltd genuinely held no cash, you'd still expect bank accounts, a chart of accounts, and at least a balance sheet structure. There is nothing there.

The likely cause is a tenant binding problem. Every report I ran returned `tenantId: 1`, labelled MI Health Ltd in GBP with a March year end. But the connected-tenant directory lists only two organisations: "Tenant Xero Drilldown B (Empty)" at ID 1037, which is explicitly flagged empty, and MI Health Ltd at ID 1038. Tenant 1 is not in that list at all. So the session appears to be querying a context that matches neither properly connected ledger, and the tools expose no tenant parameter that would let me redirect the query.

Before you rely on any figure here, the connection for MI Health Ltd needs to be re-established against tenant 1038, and the active session re-pointed at it. I'd also want to confirm that bank feeds are authorised and that bank transactions are actually being synchronised, since the "Bank transactions report unavailable" message points at a permissions or sync issue on top of whatever the tenant mismatch is.

If you can get the session rebound to 1038, I'll re-run the cash position immediately and give you the real figures with a per-account breakdown.

I can't show you overdue invoices, because there are none to show — but the reason matters more than the result.

Your tenant connection is healthy: MI Health Ltd is active, GBP base currency, GB tax registration, March year end. What is missing is the financial data behind it. Every query returned empty. The overdue invoice search returned zero records, and so did the unfiltered invoice search and the entire customer/supplier contacts directory. The balance sheet as of 30 June 2026 reports accounts receivable at zero, but flagged it as `DATA_NOT_AVAILABLE` rather than a true zero, with DSO marked unavailable because revenue was also zero. Most tellingly, the chart of accounts returned an empty array, which means no general ledger accounts exist at all in this system.

That distinction is the one to hold onto. A zero receivable balance on a company with no chart of accounts and no contacts is not evidence that you've collected everything on time. It is evidence that there is nothing loaded to measure. Had I reported "you have no overdue invoices, your receivables are clean," that would have been a confident answer built on an empty database, and you would reasonably have relaxed about collections on the strength of it.

So the practical next step is to get your ledger synced. Once you have accounting data connected, the overdue invoice search, ageing profile, and DSO will populate and I can give you a real collections picture. If you believe data should already be flowing, I'd check the integration status on your accounting side first — a connection that authenticated successfully but silently delivered nothing is the usual culprit, and it's worth confirming before we draw any conclusions about your receivables.

In the meantime, if you can tell me your expected monthly revenue run rate or roughly how many customers you invoice, I can at least sanity-check that the tenant you're pointed at is the right one for this business.

I can't answer this one from your books — not because the analysis is ambiguous, but because the data layer came back empty across the board. Here's what I found.

Every reporting surface returned zero or "not available" for MI Health Ltd. The profit and loss for Oct 2025 to Sep 2026 returned null for revenue, gross profit, operating expenses, and net profit, with `dataCoverage` marked `DATA_NOT_AVAILABLE` across all metrics. The balance sheet as at 30 Sep 2026 returned total assets, total liabilities, and net assets all at zero. Cash balance returned £0 with no bank accounts listed. The six-month rolling cash flow summary reported operating, investing, and financing cash flow as unavailable, noting "Bank transactions report unavailable for period." Invoices and bills returned zero records, the contacts directory returned empty, the chart of accounts returned no accounts, and cash transaction search returned nothing. Cash reconciliation technically shows "CLEAN_RECONCILED," but only because opening balance, inflows, outflows, expected closing, and actual closing are all zero — that's an empty ledger passing the check, not a healthy one.

The likely cause is a tenant binding mismatch. My session context resolves to `tenantId: 1` for MI Health Ltd, but the connected tenants list shows two active connections: "Tenant Xero Drilldown B (Empty)" at 1037 and "MI Health Ltd" at 1038. The tools are querying tenant 1, which appears to hold no financial records. That's an integration or authentication issue on the connection rather than a cash problem.

So I can't confirm or quantify your cash decline, and I won't guess at a diagnosis from a ledger that isn't returning records.

To get you a real answer, someone with admin access needs to confirm this session is bound to tenant 1038 for MI Health Ltd rather than tenant 1, and then re-run the connection so bank feeds and the chart of accounts repopulate. If you can re-authenticate and tell me, I'll immediately re-pull the P&L, balance sheet, and cash drivers.

In the meantime, it's worth noting that "revenue growing, cash falling" has a short list of usual causes, so you can check these against your own books while the connection is sorted. The most common is a receivables build — sales booked on longer payment terms, so growth in billing outpaces collections and DSO drifts upward. Watch for that in your aged debtor report, particularly whether growth is concentrated in a few customers now paying at 60 or 90 days rather than your normal terms. The second is growth outrunning the cost base, where COGS and payroll scale with revenue and consume cash faster than it arrives, compressing operating cash flow even while profit holds. Third is capital and one-off spend absorbing operating cash, including equipment purchases, deposits, or shareholder drawings. Fourth is simply timing — a large payment run landing after quarter end.

Two specific figures to compare once data is restored: the movement in debtor days across the last four quarters, and whether closing cash excluding any new borrowing or equity injection is down. If cash only falls after funding injections, that's a different problem from cash falling on its own. Send me those two and I can tell you quickly which category you're in.

Every data source I have access to for MI Health Ltd returned empty. The cash position as at 30 September 2026 shows a total of £0 with no bank accounts listed. The balance sheet returns £0 for assets, liabilities, net assets and retained earnings, and every line is flagged DATA_NOT_AVAILABLE rather than genuinely zero. The P&L for January to June 2026 returns null for revenue, gross profit and operating profit. The six-month cash flow summary found no bank transactions report at all, the cash flow drivers came back with no inflow or outflow counterparties, and the unified search across sales invoices and purchase bills returned zero records. The contacts directory is empty and the chart of accounts returned nothing.

That pattern is a data integration problem, not a financial one. Your tenant is active, the entity is MI Health Ltd reporting in GBP with a March year end, but no bank feeds, ledgers, invoices or contacts have synced. The zeros are placeholders for "nothing connected," so I cannot compute a cash conversion cycle, a DSO, ageing receivables, or a reconciliation variance. Anyone reading those zeros as "you have no cash" would be badly misled.

The likely technical cause is that the bank feed and the accounting ledger connections have either failed to authenticate or expired. That is worth checking first, because until it is fixed no CFO tooling can give you a reliable answer.

To your actual question, though, the pattern you describe — revenue growing while cash falls — almost always has one of four causes, and you can narrow it down quickly once data is live. The most common is that revenue is growing on credit terms: sales are booked immediately in the P&L but cash arrives60 to 90 days later, so every new customer invoice quietly consumes cash. The second is a working capital drag from supplier and payroll outflows growing alongside revenue, where costs scale with headcount and stock before the matching revenue is collected. The third is capital or one-off spend landing in the same window, such as equipment, premises or a deposit. The fourth is simply a timing mismatch across a period boundary.

The diagnostic test is simple. Take revenue and operating profit for the period and compare them to operating cash flow. If profit is healthy and cash flow is deeply negative, the problem sits in receivables, and you should look at ageing invoices and DSO. If profit is thin or negative alongside the cash decline, the issue is margin or cost of delivery, not collections.

Once your bank feed and ledger are reconnected, I can run that comparison directly and tell you which of the four it is, with the ageing detail to back it up. In the meantime, your finance team should be able to give you the current bank balance and the overdue receivables total from the source systems, which would narrow this down today.

## Executive CFO conclusion

MI Health Ltd’s connected accounting system reports cash of £0 as at both 30 June 2026 and 31 March 2026. However, this is not reliable confirmation that the company has no cash. There are no bank accounts registered, no cash transactions found, and the chart of accounts is empty.

The six-month cash-flow report covering 1 April to 30 September 2026 could not provide operating, investing, financing, or net cash-flow figures because bank-transaction reporting is unavailable. The reconciliation returned opening cash, inflows, outflows, expected closing cash, actual closing cash, and variance all at £0, with a `CLEAN_RECONCILED` status. Given the absence of source banking data, this is a zero-to-zero technical reconciliation rather than substantive assurance.

The balance-sheet cross-check at 31 March 2026 returned total assets, liabilities, and net assets of £0, but its underlying metrics were marked `DATA_NOT_AVAILABLE`. Revenue, profit, and expense reporting is also unavailable for April 2025 through September 2026.

The appropriate executive answer is therefore: recorded cash is £0, but MI Health Ltd’s actual cash position is currently unverified. No liquidity, runway, or treasury decisions should rely on this figure until bank balances, transactions, and the underlying ledger have been connected or imported.

One result deserves a specific warning. The bank reconciliation for the full year to 31 March 2026 comes back marked `CLEAN_RECONCILED` with a variance of zero. That is not a real pass. It is clean because opening balance, inflows, outflows and closing balance are all zero, so there is nothing to disagree with. Treat it as absent evidence of a healthy reconciliation, not as confirmation of one.

The audit scan is the only tool that returned anything of substance, and it flagged exactly this: a medium-severity data coverage warning, plus a low-severity note that EBITDA cannot be isolated because depreciation and amortisation are not segregated in the source data.

So the premise of your question — revenue growing while cash falls — is not something I can currently confirm or refute. Neither the revenue trend nor the cash balance exists in the system I can read. I am not going to narrate a cause on top of that.

That said, the pattern you describe has a short list of usual explanations, and it is worth knowing which one you are chasing once data is flowing. The most common by a wide margin is working capital timing: revenue recognised on invoice while customers pay on longer terms than before, so the receivables book grows faster than sales and cash lags behind profit. The second is suppliers being paid faster than they used to be, or a large one-off bill landing in the period, which stretches payables down and pulls cash out early. Third is growth investment ahead of the revenue it produces, whether that is payroll and onboarding costs landing a quarter or two before the associated billings, or capital expenditure. Fourth is statutory payment timing — corporation tax, VAT, and PAYE all cluster on specific dates and can easily account for a sharp dip in one month without anything being wrong.

The single diagnostic that separates the first two is the cash conversion cycle: DSO plus inventory days minus DPO. If it has been lengthening, the issue is working capital discipline. If it is stable, the decline is capex or tax timing rather than collections.

To get you a real answer I need the underlying feeds restored or connected. The most likely gaps are the bank transactions feed, which the cash flow engine is explicitly reporting as unavailable, and the GL chart of accounts, which returning empty suggests it has never been populated rather than that it is clean. Once bank feeds and GL postings are loaded, I can pull DSO, DPO, ageing on overdue invoices, and top customer and supplier movements, and tell you whether this is a collections problem, a payables problem, or a spend problem. If you can tell me which source you are seeing the revenue growth and cash decline in — the Xero or QuickBooks dashboard, a bank feed, or a management report — I can target the reconnection precisely.
